column4: This is the section's clearest full arc: the verse names the staged making of the embryo and then says some are “يُرَدُّ ... أَرْذَلَ ٱلْعُمُرِ,” returned to the feeblest age, losing knowledge; it then turns to dead earth stirred by rain as another sign of resurrection. The source section explicitly reads the named root ر د د as a return along life's course.
The verse uses “يُرَدُّ” for those returned to the feeblest age, where knowledge fades after having been known. That directly supplies the old-age reading of the source section's root ر د د in 95:5.
The verse traces people from weakness to strength and back to weakness and gray hair, matching the section's rising and declining bodily course.
It says that one given long life is “نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ,” turned back in creation. This is the section's aging reversal after the body's best form; it states the reversal directly.
The verse lays out the course from dust and a drop to birth, maturity, old age, and an appointed term, giving a fuller lifespan sequence alongside the section's account.
The phrase “خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ” describes creation after creation in the wombs, matching the section's staged development and its discussion of the خ ل ق root.

The source section links the mountain-name ṭūr in 95:2 with its dictionary form ṭawr, “stage,” by sound rather than by the oath's meaning. Noah's “أَطْوَارًا” uses that root in the actual sense of humans being made in stages.
The verse moves from dust to a drop, then speaks of conception, birth, maturity, and a lifespan being shortened or extended. It makes life's bodily stages and measured duration explicit.
The sequence begins with man's origin from clay, matching the first material stage named in the source section's account of 22:5.
The drop placed in a secure lodging continues the bodily-development sequence that the section traces from the womb onward.

This verse gives the stages from a clinging form through a lump, bones, and flesh, then says “ثُمَّ أَنشَأْنَٰهُ خَلْقًا ءَاخَرَ” and praises Allah as “أَحْسَنُ ٱلْخَٰلِقِينَ.” The section explicitly joins this staged making and the phrase “best of creators” to its account of human form.
Following the formation sequence in 23:12–14, this verse says that people die afterward, matching the section's transition from life's stages to death cutting off its span.

After the death named in 23:15, this verse says people will be raised on Resurrection Day. That completes the creation-to-death-to-return sequence which the source section reads as a case for judgment.
The verse asks whether man was not a drop of emitted fluid, a first bodily stage that begins the same surah's creation-to-resurrection argument.
It moves from the drop to a clinging form and says God created and proportioned him, directly paralleling the section's developmental stages and completed bodily form.
The verse continues the formation sequence by making the two sexes, another concrete stage in the creation argument.

After the drop, clinging form, and formation in 75:37–39, the verse asks whether that Creator can give life to the dead. Its own contribution is the explicit resurrection conclusion the section draws after displaying life's stages.

In response to a man's denial of the Hour, the companion recalls that God made him from dust, then a drop, then formed him as a man. That staged origin is used as a direct answer to denial, as in the section's final question.
It traces gestation and nursing to maturity and the age of forty, making pregnancy, growth, and adulthood part of a human lifespan sequence.
The verse says God created, proportioned, and balanced the human being (“خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ”), a close parallel to the section's reading of taqwīm as completed bodily form.
It completes the preceding formation statement by saying God assembled man in whatever form He willed, giving the section's account of formed bodily shape a direct counterpart.
The verse says God created and formed people and made their forms good (“وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ”), directly echoing the section's claim that the human form reaches its best completion.
It says God formed people and made their forms good, a direct parallel to the section's account of the human body's completed form.

This follows the staged creation and revived-earth scene in 22:5 and states their conclusion: God is the Truth and gives life to the dead. This is the verse's own contribution to the section's resurrection reading.
Following 22:5–6, this verse says the Hour is coming and God will raise those in the graves. It supplies the judgment claim that the section asks how anyone could deny after seeing life's stages.

The verse asks how people disbelieve in God after being lifeless, brought to life, made to die, given life again, and returned to Him. This compact life-death-return sequence echoes the section's stages and its closing challenge about denial.

The verse pairs a humbled earth stirred by rain with God's power to give life to the dead. This is a close counterpart to the dead ground revived at the end of 22:5, which the section treats as resurrection evidence.

It says that God revives a dead land with measured rain and immediately adds, “كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ,” likewise you will be brought forth. That makes explicit the earth-to-resurrection link noted in the section's reading of 22:5.
The verse asks the reader to see how God gives life to earth after its death and then says He gives life to the dead. It develops the same rain-revived-earth proof that the section notices in 22:5.

After rain-grown gardens and grain in 50:9–10, this verse calls the revival of dead land provision and says, “كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ,” thus is the emergence. It completes the same soil-to-resurrection scene mentioned in the section.
The verse says rain gives life to earth after its death. It is a direct parallel to the revived dry ground that the section identifies as part of 22:5's proof.
It tells listeners that God gives life to earth after its death, another direct formulation of the land-revival image developed through 22:5.
The verse names dead earth revived to produce grain as a sign. This is a specific parallel to the rain-stirred land at the end of 22:5 in the section's resurrection argument.

The verse describes the challenge about rotten bones (“وَهِىَ رَمِيمٌ”) and says the challenger forgot his own creation (“خَلْقَهُ”). The source section names خ ل ق's dictionary branch for things becoming worn; this verse makes bodily decay and forgotten creation the concrete issue.
This answers the rotten-bones question in 36:78 by saying the One who created them the first time will give them life. It completes the decay-and-return connection in the preceding verse.
The verse says God has ordained death among people and cannot be thwarted, directly matching the section's claim that death cuts off a human lifespan.

It continues that death statement by saying God can replace people and bring them forth in a form they do not know. This makes the section's changing bodily form and return part of a larger creation argument.
Following death and transformation in 56:60–61, the verse recalls the first creation and asks why people do not take heed. It explicitly ties the known life-course to God's power to create anew.
It names man as created from a gushing fluid, a bodily origin stage that begins this passage's argument about return.
The verse specifies where that fluid emerges, continuing the creation detail that the section's staged-development image calls to mind.
After the account of human origin in 86:5–7, it says God is surely able to return man. This is the passage's explicit creation-to-return inference.

The verse asks whether God was wearied by the first creation and says the deniers are confused about a new creation. The contrast between the completed first making and denied return directly answers the section's challenge after life's stages.

The verse records the objection that people will be recreated after being lost in the earth. This is the same denial of return from a body's dissolution that the section's creation-to-death arc puts in question.
It answers the objection in 32:10 by naming the Angel of Death and saying people will be returned to their Lord, completing the body's death-to-return sequence.

The verse quotes people asking whether they will be raised after becoming bones and fragments. That body-wearing image corresponds to the source section's dictionary branch of خ ل ق for something worn out.

In the 17:49–51 exchange, 17:49 raises the objection about bones and fragments; this verse asks “مَن يُعِيدُنَا,” who will restore the deniers after dissolution. Its own wording directly meets the section's return-root ر د د and its old-age/death arc.
This verse restates denial after becoming bones and fragments, asking whether people will be raised as a new creation. It makes the section's worn-body and return contrast explicit.

Following the denial in 17:98, it argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth can create the like of them. This completes the first-creation/new-creation answer relevant to the section's staged making.

The deniers say that after bodies have disintegrated in the earth, they will be in a new creation. This gives a direct bodily-decay counterpart to the source section's named worn-out sense of خ ل ق and its question about return.
The verse cites deniers asking whether they will be in a new creation after becoming dust, a direct reversal of the source section's dust-to-human beginning and a challenge to its return sequence.
The verse asks whether people will be raised after death as dust and bones, connecting bodily decay to the return that follows the section's lifespan arc.
The verse quotes deniers asking whether they will be raised after becoming dust and bones, directly matching the section's passage from formed life to death and disputed return.
The verse quotes the objection that people will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones, a direct bodily-decay version of the denial challenged by the section.
This continues the objection in 23:82 by dismissing the promised resurrection as an old tale. It makes the denial of the return explicit in the same creation-and-death context.
The verse voices the objection that decayed bones could not be restored, directly connecting bodily wearing and the denied return to the section's lifecourse.
This continues 79:11 by calling such restoration a losing return, explicitly naming the return that the section's final question says remains to be denied.
The verse says every soul will taste death and then be returned to God, a concise version of the section's life-ending and onward-return sequence.
It says every soul tastes death and that recompense is completed on Resurrection Day. This links the end of the bodily course to the judgment and reward that remain beyond it.

The verse contrasts what people possess, which runs out, with what is with God, which remains, and promises the patient their reward. This concretely parallels the section's cut-off lifespan beside an “uninterrupted reward.”
The verse promises believers and doers of good an “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ,” the same phrase as 95:6 and the section's contrast between a life cut short and an uncut reward.
It gives the same promise of “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ” to those who believe and do good, directly echoing the reward phrase the section sets against death.
The verse promises the Prophet “لَأَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ,” using the same uncut-reward wording that the section contrasts with the span of mortal life.

The verse contrasts the enjoyment of worldly life with what is better and more lasting with God. It makes explicit the passing-life/lasting-reward distinction that the section draws from death and “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.”
The verse says people prefer worldly life. Against the source section's mortal course ending in death, this stance gives a concrete reason someone might neglect the lasting reward it describes.
It says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, a direct contrast to the mortal lifespan beside the section's uncut reward.

The verse quotes people who say only worldly life exists, that they die and live, and that time destroys them. This is the explicit denial of any return against which the section's life stages and final question are set.

The verse reports the claim that the dead will not be raised and answers that they certainly will. That is the precise denial of the return the section challenges after laying out human creation and death.

The speaker says he does not think the Hour will come; 18:37 answers with his creation from dust, a drop, and full human form. This denial supplies the exact stance the section's staged-creation argument addresses.

The verse asks whether people thought they were created without purpose and would not be returned. It gives the return-purpose question that the section's closing challenge raises after the life-course has been displayed.

The section identifies 95:2's طُور as the mountain in the oath and links its sound to the source-section dictionary form ṭawr, “stage.” 52:1 again swears by “ٱلطُّورِ”; it preserves the mountain-oath half of that image, though its local argument is not about bodily stages.

This verse begins the rain-to-growth passage completed in 50:11: water grows gardens and grain, while 50:11 supplies the explicit dead-land-to-emergence link. Its own rain-grown land scene parallels the revived ground the section notes in 22:5.

The source section names غ ي ر and a dictionary sense of changing a thing's outward state while its essence remains. This verse uses the root for a people changing their condition; the sense is moral and social rather than bodily aging, but it offers a specific parallel of continuing identity through changed state.

The source section distinguishes the negating word غَيْرُ from its root's sense of alteration. This verse uses the root for a favor's condition changing when people change themselves; the connection to bodily aging is indirect, since its context is a community's moral state.
The verse says God fashions people in the wombs as He wills. That directly extends the section's formed and unformed embryo detail and its account of bodily form taking shape.

The verse says God knows what every female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, with all things measured by Him. It adds the womb's changing development and measure to the staged formation discussed in the section.

People are brought from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and hearts. This supplies the beginning-of-life knowledge state that contrasts specifically with 22:5 and 16:70, where old age may return a person to knowing nothing.

After 40:67 traces birth, maturity, old age, and a term, this verse says God gives life and causes death and that His command brings things into being. Its own contribution is to state the divine life-and-death power behind that lifespan.
It says man was created from a clinging clot, a specific womb stage also named in the source section's staged account; the source section's root خ ل ق is used here for making.
The verse says man was created from a mixed drop to be tested and given hearing and sight, adding a concrete beginning-of-life stage to the section's human-development arc.
It asks whether people were not created from a lowly fluid, directly naming the initial bodily material in the section's staged account.
The verse says that fluid was placed in a secure lodging, supplying a specific womb detail alongside the section's formed and unformed stages.

After 77:20–21 names the fluid and its lodging, this verse says it remains there until a known term. Its contribution is the measured duration of gestation that joins the section's developmental stages to time.
Following the fluid, lodging, and term in 77:20–22, this verse says God measured it. It makes the measured ordering of bodily development explicit.

The verse says man was created from a drop and proportioned. It joins the section's initial developmental material to its claim that human form is brought to completion; the source section names خ ل ق for that making.
It says God began man's creation from clay, another statement of the material beginning that the section includes in its account of human stages.
It says human descendants were made from an extract of fluid, adding the reproductive beginning to the clay origin in 32:7 and to the section's staged development.
It says God fashioned the human and gave hearing, sight, and hearts, a specific completion of bodily formation that complements the section's reading of taqwīm as achieved form.
The verse says God created people, setting up the passage's challenge about who creates human life that the section treats as a visible sequence of stages.
It asks the reader to consider the fluid people emit, naming a concrete reproductive beginning that corresponds to the section's drop-to-embryo progression.

After 56:58 asks about emitted fluid, this verse asks whether people create it or God is its Creator. Its own contribution is to make human formation an argument about the Creator, like the section's use of the stages before its challenge to denial.
The verse names creation from an emitted drop, a repeated Qur'anic formulation of the early bodily stage that the section traces through the womb.
The verse states that God gave people life, then causes death, then gives life again. This is a compact counterpart to the section's life-course ending in death and its question about return.

The verse asks who originates creation and repeats it, then also asks who brings water and revives the earth. It brings together both images developed in the section: human creation and land revived after death.
Among the signs named here is rain by which God gives life to earth after its death. This repeats the dead-ground scene the section notices in 22:5, placing it among signs for those who reason.
The verse says God gives life, causes death, and gathers people for the Day of Resurrection. It directly answers the mortal course in the section with the return that follows it.

It says God created people from clay and appointed a term, then remarks that they still doubt. This connects the section's creation and measured lifespan to the very denial its closing question addresses.

The verse describes a mother carrying a child through weakness upon weakness and weaning him over two years. It supplies gestation and infancy as concrete stages within the section's wider life-course image.

The verse says Moses reached maturity and full strength before being given judgment and knowledge. This is a specific instance of the adult-strength stage that the section places between early life and old age, though the local passage is Moses' biography.

It asks whether people have not seen how God originates creation and then repeats it. This is another explicit creation-to-re-creation formulation of the inference the section draws from human stages.
The verse says God originates creation and then repeats it, and that this is easy for Him. It gives a direct repeated-creation counterpart to the section's staged creation and return.

The verse asks whether any of the partners can originate creation and then repeat it, and answers that God does so. It turns creation and return into a direct challenge about who has that power, like the section's final challenge after the life stages.
The verse says God gives life and death and that to Him people return. This directly states the life-ending and return sequence developed by the section.

The verse describes rain used to revive a dead land and provide water for people and animals. The dead-land scene is a specific parallel to the closing sign in 22:5 that the section connects with resurrection.

The verse asks who sends rain and revives the earth after its death; the answer given is Allah. Its own contribution is the recognition of the same dead-land revival scene the section reads as evidence beyond ordinary decline.
The verse lists rain from heaven and the earth revived after its death among God's signs. This repeats the precise land-revival image the section identifies at the end of 22:5.

The verse calls worldly life passing amusement and says the true life is the Hereafter. It makes explicit the finite-life/lasting-beyond-it contrast that the section develops through death and an uncut reward.

The source section names م ن ن in the phrase for an uncut reward and also gives “al-manūn” as a death that cuts life's span. This verse says opponents await “رَيْبَ ٱلْمَنُونِ” for the Prophet; the phrase can mean a turn of fate or time's calamity, including death, so its connection to the section's death sense is plausible but lexically less certain.
